nodes.label: Air-gapped transaction signing
nodes.rationale: The sketch shows physical controls and a screen instead of any tethered interface, implying the signing workflow is designed to run without a live data connection between wallet and computer.

nodes.label: COLDCARD Hardware Wallet (keypad + green screen)
nodes.rationale: Technical watercolor sketch of a Coldcard: the 12-button physical keypad plus a small monochrome screen means the PIN and transaction details are entered and verified entirely on the device, so the host computer never sees secrets. Hardware is visible through screws and a USB-C port, signalling a manufactured (not purely conceptual) product.

nodes.label: On-device numeric keypad for PIN entry
nodes.norm_label: on-device numeric keypad for pin entry
nodes.rationale: A telephone-style keypad (1-9, lock, 0, X) allows the PIN to be typed directly on the wallet, removing the need for a companion app or host keyboard that could log the entry.

nodes.label: Blockstream Jade Hardware Wallet
nodes.rationale: Rendered as a two-material enclosure: a dark textured half holding a circular lens/sensor and a lighter metallic half with a diamond logo and pill button. The lens is the distinguishing physical feature of an air-gapped wallet that exchanges data by scanning QR codes.

nodes.label: QR-code based air-gapped data exchange
nodes.rationale: A camera lens on the device implies transaction data is transferred optically rather than over USB, preserving the air gap while still letting the wallet read what it signs.

nodes.label: Ledger Nano Hardware Wallet
nodes.rationale: Drawn as an open two-part USB-stick form factor (translucent screen section plus metallic body), the design prioritises portability and a small screen that shows only what must be confirmed.

nodes.label: Multi-asset support shown on screen
nodes.rationale: The screen lists Bitcoin plus several other coin/token icons, communicating that one device manages many chains rather than a single-asset wallet.

nodes.label: TREZOR Hardware Wallet (Model One style)
nodes.rationale: Rendered with a brand label plus padlock icon, a green OLED screen showing the Bitcoin symbol over circuit traces, and a bottom-edge cable; the circuit-trace motif stresses that the device holds keys and performs signing itself.

nodes.label: Two-button on-device confirmation
nodes.rationale: Two rectangular buttons under the screen implement confirm/deny without a full keypad, keeping the device small while still requiring a physical action for every transaction.

nodes.label: Multi-brand hardware wallet lineup
nodes.rationale: Photographing Coldcard, Ledger, Trezor and KeepKey together frames the hardware wallet market as a comparison across form factors (keypad, USB stick, button pad) rather than a single recommended device.

nodes.label: USB-tethered form factor
nodes.rationale: Visible USB cables and stick-shaped bodies show that most of these wallets depend on a host computer both for power and for relaying signed transactions.

nodes.label: Unlabeled fourth device (dual-tone, lens, diamond logo)
nodes.norm_label: unlabeled fourth device (dual-tone, lens, diamond logo)

nodes.label: Comparative critique of hardware wallet designs
nodes.norm_label: comparative critique of hardware wallet designs
nodes.rationale: The four devices are presented together under a critical title, so the image is a visual argument: each form factor (numeric keypad, two-button, USB stick, camera-equipped) is being weighed for where it compromises security or usability rather than simply displayed.

nodes.label: Next.js Breaking Changes Warning
nodes.rationale: The installed Next.js version diverges from model training data, so APIs, conventions, and file structure may differ; agents must consult bundled docs instead of assuming prior knowledge. Hedging on stale knowledge avoids generating code against removed or changed APIs.

nodes.label: Read Bundled Next.js Docs Requirement
nodes.rationale: Guides are resolved from node_modules/next/dist/docs/ relative to the instruction file's directory because in monorepos the next package may not be visible from the repo root. Reading local, version-matched docs is authoritative over memory, and deprecation notices must be heeded.

nodes.label: Commit Managed Block to Keep Tree Clean
nodes.norm_label: commit managed block to keep tree clean
nodes.rationale: Editing the block out of a diff only causes next dev to re-add it as an uncommitted change, so committing it alongside work keeps the working tree clean and avoids perpetual diff noise.

nodes.label: Chamfered Corner Frame Motif
nodes.rationale: Angled corners replace rounded ones to suggest precision machining and tamper-evident hardware, reinforcing physical security cues.

nodes.label: Viewfinder Corner Brackets
nodes.rationale: Open corners imply scanning/surveillance framing, visually pairing a ledger/record metaphor with the idea of monitored verification.

nodes.label: Geometric Block Icon
nodes.rationale: A horizontal bar over two separated vertical blocks abstracts a stacked card/chip; the gap between blocks hints at a physical seam, i.e. a card you tap or split.

nodes.label: Padlock Shield Icon
nodes.rationale: U-shaped shackle over an angled shield body merges two security archetypes - locking and armour - into one silhouette that survives monochrome rendering.

nodes.label: Coldcard Brand Logo
nodes.rationale: Minimal flat single-color mark: the 'CODECARD' wordmark is set inside a chamfered-corner red frame on white, so the asset stays legible at small icon sizes and reads as an engraved, industrial plaque - fitting a security-hardware brand.

nodes.label: Ledger Brand Logo
nodes.rationale: Black uppercase wordmark framed by four bracket-like corner marks; the framing acts as a viewfinder that centers attention on the name while keeping the mark monochrome for any background.

nodes.label: Tangem Brand Logo
nodes.rationale: Icon-plus-lowercase-wordmark lockup in solid black; the lowercase, rounded-geometric type signals a consumer-friendly card form factor rather than industrial hardware.

nodes.label: Trezor Brand Logo
nodes.rationale: Bold uppercase wordmark paired with a shield-shaped padlock icon, making the security promise (locking away keys) explicit in the mark itself.

nodes.label: Architecture Diagram
nodes.rationale: Over-simplified trust-boundary sketch of the Trezor Safe 5: firmware only runs after the secure element checks its signature, the host app never touches the seed, and only a signature travels back to the host.

nodes.label: Encrypted Seed in Device Flash
nodes.rationale: Stored encrypted on the device flash and never leaves the device.

nodes.label: Open-source Firmware
nodes.rationale: Open-source image signed by Trezor; the device boots it only after the secure element validates the signature, which is the defense against malicious firmware.

nodes.label: Host App (Trezor Suite on Computer/Phone)
nodes.rationale: Builds the transaction payload and broadcasts it; it never touches the seed and only receives a signature, keeping key material off the general-purpose OS.

nodes.label: Malicious Firmware Section
nodes.rationale: Threat-model section beginning below the use cases; pairs the attack ('happens without you approving it on the device') with the signature check that blocks it.

nodes.label: Microcontroller
nodes.rationale: Runs the firmware and implements replay protection, sitting between the host link, the secure element, the display and the flash storage.

nodes.label: Secure Element
nodes.rationale: Verifies the firmware signature and guards the PIN, so a compromised main MCU still cannot boot unsigned code or extract the PIN.

nodes.label: Touchscreen + Haptics (On-device Confirmation)
nodes.rationale: The payout confirmation surface: the annotation 'you confirm every payout here' makes the display the last line of defense against a malicious host.

nodes.label: Trezor Safe 5 Device
nodes.rationale: USB-C hardware wallet with secure element and color touchscreen; drawn as a dashed enclosure so everything inside ships on the device.

nodes.label: Use Cases Diagram
nodes.rationale: Tree from a single actor ('You') into three lifecycle columns, each holding three tasks; conveys that every action is approved on the device itself.

nodes.label: Create a New Wallet
nodes.rationale: 20-word backup, written on paper.

nodes.label: Malicious Firmware Heading at Fold
nodes.rationale: Only the heading and its large display type are visible, showing the section is separated by generous whitespace rather than a rule or card.

nodes.label: Recover from a Backup
nodes.rationale: Type the recovery words on the device itself, never into the host.

nodes.label: Set a PIN
nodes.rationale: Asked every time the device wakes up; guarded by the secure element.

nodes.label: Share a Receive Address
nodes.rationale: Confirm the address on the display to defeat host-side address swapping.

nodes.label: Sign a Payment
nodes.rationale: Check address and fee on screen before approving.

nodes.label: Docked Navigation Over Content
nodes.rationale: The nav bar is fixed and floats over the scrolling content with a translucent white background, so diagram content passes underneath it.

nodes.label: Unlock with a Passphrase
nodes.rationale: One hidden wallet per passphrase, so unlock doubles as wallet selection.

nodes.label: Update the Firmware
nodes.rationale: Signed by Trezor and checked on the device.

nodes.label: Nine Use-Case Task Cards
nodes.rationale: Each card is a title plus one-line 'what it asks of you' subtitle, so the device-side confirmation is always stated next to the task.

nodes.label: Verify the Device
nodes.rationale: Suite checks the firmware signature, reusing the boot-time trust check as a user-facing verification step.

nodes.label: Wipe Before Selling
nodes.rationale: Factory reset drops the seed, the terminal step of the seed lifecycle.

nodes.label: Canvas Zoom / Fit Controls
nodes.rationale: Plus, minus and fit-to-screen buttons let the same diagram scale down on mobile without a separate mobile layout.

nodes.label: Empty Whitespace Region
nodes.rationale: No diagram content occupies this band; the airy spacing mirrors the page's section separation but costs scroll length.

nodes.label: Bottom Nav with Profile Avatar
nodes.rationale: Avatar on the far left balances three trailing icons, giving the bar an asymmetric anchor rather than centring the nav items.

nodes.label: Docked Bar Sliver (Partial Render)
nodes.rationale: Partially painted nav elements suggest the screenshot caught the page mid-render or scrolled past the content.

nodes.label: Diagram Prototype Page (Trezor Safe 5)
nodes.rationale: Scratch page for iterating on diagram drawings: three stacked diagram sections (Architecture, Use cases, Malicious firmware) share one legend vocabulary and a persistent bottom navigation dock.

nodes.label: Use-Case Section Viewport
nodes.rationale: Close-up capture of the use-case section: the nine task cards sit inside the dotted canvas frame with zoom controls, the legend follows, and the 'Malicious firmware' heading enters at the fold.

nodes.label: Mostly Empty Canvas Capture
nodes.rationale: Capture of an unused layout region: blank white field with only the docked navigation visible, indicating large vertical gaps between diagram sections.

nodes.label: Bottom Navigation Close-up
nodes.rationale: Cropped view of the docked bar: avatar pinned left, Home/Academy/globe group offset right, faint separators instead of a hard scrim.

nodes.label: Blank Viewport with Bar Sliver
nodes.rationale: Nearly unrendered frame: only a thin strip of the docked bar shows along the bottom edge, with a stray disclosure caret above it.

nodes.label: Shared Diagram Legend
nodes.rationale: Colour/shape vocabulary (host, firmware, storage, hardware, security, dashed enclosure) reused by every section so a reader learns it once.

nodes.label: Single-Actor, Device-Approved Interaction Model
nodes.rationale: Design intent: one actor ('You') exists and every action is approved on the device, so the host can be untrusted without changing the user's mental model.

nodes.label: Set up / Everyday Use / Upkeep Grouping
nodes.norm_label: set up / everyday use / upkeep grouping
nodes.rationale: Grouping is temporal rather than feature-based: when the interaction happens decides the column, which keeps nine tasks scannable in three rows.

nodes.label: Legend Block Below Diagram
nodes.rationale: Legend is placed after the drawing, not in a side rail, because the diagram is full-width and scroll-heavy on small screens.
